about: How new ventures come to pivot through a series of smaller decisions, often prompted by unanticipated opportunities met after founding, rather than one planned change.

candidates.label: Unanticipated opportunity after founding
candidates.definition: After the venture is started, an opportunity the founders did not anticipate appears and starts a change of direction.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes an opportunity they had not looked for that arose once the venture was running.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The new direction came from a planned search or a scheduled strategy review.

candidates.label: Casual conversation reveals an opportunity
candidates.definition: An informal conversation, not aimed at the venture's strategy, surfaces a new possibility.
candidates.applies_when: The founder credits an offhand or social conversation with revealing an opportunity.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The conversation was a planned customer interview or pitch.

candidates.label: Unsolicited approach from outside
candidates.definition: A customer, partner or other party approaches the venture unasked with a request or offer that opens a new direction.
candidates.applies_when: Someone outside contacts the founder on their own initiative with an offer or request.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The founder sought out the contact.

candidates.label: Discovery during own product work
candidates.definition: While developing their own product, the team finds something that suggests a different use or market.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes finding a new possibility in the course of building or testing their product.

candidates.label: Pivot that accumulates over steps
candidates.definition: The change of direction builds up through several smaller decisions rather than one deliberate switch.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes a series of small moves that together amounted to a new direction.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: A single, planned decision changed the venture's direction.

candidates.label: Expanding beliefs and language
candidates.definition: Founders widen what they believe the venture is and how they describe it, which lets the new opportunity fit.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes redefining what the company does, or changing how they talk about it, to take in a new opportunity.

candidates.label: Considering a change and deciding against it
candidates.definition: After a trigger, firms often consider changing strategy and then reject the change, keeping their strategy with at most small adjustments.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes weighing an unexpected problem or opportunity and choosing not to change course.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The founder never noticed or considered the opportunity at all.

candidates.label: Acting in the market surfaces opportunities
candidates.definition: Opportunities appear because the founders are actively doing things in the market, not by waiting or planning.
candidates.applies_when: The founder links the opportunity to activity already under way, such as selling or building.

candidates.label: Pivot named only in hindsight
candidates.definition: Founders recognise and label the change as a pivot only after it has happened.
candidates.applies_when: The founder says they only realised later that they had changed direction.

candidates.label: Board resists tangents
candidates.definition: Investors or board members discourage the founders from following side opportunities, even surprising ones.
candidates.applies_when: The founder describes investors or a board pushing back on following an unexpected opportunity.
